cards.subject: An entity
says: represents a kind of thing the app stores, such as a user or an order
usually becomes a table with one row per instance
cards.use: need to decide what things the system must remember
not: is always stored as a single column

cards.subject: A relationship
says: describes how two entities are connected
is one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many
cards.use: need to say that one customer can place many orders
not: exists only in application code and never in the schema

cards.subject: A one-to-many relationship
says: puts the foreign key on the many side
lets one parent row own several child rows
cards.use: model a blog post that has many comments
not: needs a junction table to work

cards.subject: A many-to-many relationship
says: cannot be stored with a single foreign key column on either table
needs a third table that links the two sides
cards.use: model students who take many courses while each course has many students
not: is stored by a comma-separated list of ids in one column

cards.subject: A junction table
says: holds one row per linked pair of records
can carry attributes of the link itself, such as an enrolment date
often uses its two foreign keys together as a composite primary key
cards.use: need to record which user enrolled in which track and when
not: holds a copy of every column from both tables it links

cards.subject: A single source of truth
says: keeps each fact stored in exactly one place
stops copies of a fact from drifting apart
cards.use: see the same value kept in three tables and disagreeing
not: means every table must store all the data it ever needs

cards.subject: A derived column
says: stores a value that could be computed from other columns
needs a rule to keep it in step with its sources
cards.use: have measured a slow aggregate and decide to store a total
not: can never become stale

cards.subject: A lookup table
says: holds a fixed list of allowed values as rows that other tables reference
lets a label change in one row without rewriting every row that uses it
cards.use: need a list of statuses that can grow without changing the schema
not: is created automatically by every foreign key

cards.subject: Storing timestamps in UTC
says: avoids ambiguity when users and servers sit in different time zones
converts to local time only when shown to a person
cards.use: run servers and users in several time zones
not: makes daylight saving changes corrupt stored values

cards.subject: An effective-dated row
says: records the period during which a value was true
lets you report what a price was last March
cards.use: need history of a value after it changes instead of overwriting it
not: overwrites the old value in place

cards.subject: A polymorphic association
says: points at rows in different tables using a type column plus an id
cannot be enforced by an ordinary foreign key
cards.use: have comments that can attach to posts, photos or videos
not: is checked by the database like any foreign key

cards.subject: A primary key
says: uniquely identifies each row in a table
is the usual target of foreign keys in other tables
cards.use: need every row to have an identity other rows can refer to
not: may repeat as long as the other columns differ

cards.subject: A foreign key
says: ties a column to the primary key of another table
blocks a child row that points at a missing parent
cards.use: need the database to refuse an order for a customer that does not exist
not: copies the parent row into the child table

cards.subject: A NOT NULL constraint
says: rejects a row that leaves the column empty
turns a required field into a rule the database enforces
cards.use: need a column such as email to always have a value
not: rejects empty strings as well as NULL

cards.subject: A UNIQUE constraint
says: rejects a second row with the same value in the column or column set
can cover several columns so only the combination must be unique
cards.use: need only one enrolment per user and track
not: makes the column the table's primary key

cards.subject: A CHECK constraint
says: rejects a row whose values fail a stated condition
can limit a column to a range or a list of allowed values
cards.use: need a price column to never be negative
not: looks up values in another table

cards.subject: A surrogate key
says: is a generated identifier with no business meaning
stays stable when real-world details change
cards.use: need an identifier that survives an email address change
not: is built from the customer's real details

cards.subject: A natural key
says: is built from real-world data such as an email or a country code
forces updates to every reference if the real-world value changes
cards.use: have a stable standard code that already identifies each row
not: is always generated by the database

cards.subject: A composite key
says: combines two or more columns to identify a row
is common in junction tables
cards.use: need the pair of two ids to be the identity of a link row
not: can only be used on tables with no foreign keys

cards.subject: An auto-increment key
says: is assigned by the database in increasing order
can reveal how many rows exist when exposed in a URL
cards.use: want simple ids handed out without the client choosing them
not: is guaranteed to have no gaps

cards.subject: A random UUID key
says: can be generated by the client without asking the database
scatters new rows across the index instead of appending to the end
cards.use: need ids created offline or in several systems before they reach the database
not: is smaller than an integer key

cards.subject: ON DELETE CASCADE
says: deletes child rows automatically when the parent row is deleted
can remove far more data than intended after a mistaken delete
cards.use: want an order's lines to disappear together with the order
not: blocks the delete when children exist

cards.subject: ON DELETE RESTRICT
says: refuses to delete a parent row while child rows still reference it
forces the caller to deal with the children first
cards.use: must protect records, such as invoices, that may not vanish with their customer
not: deletes the child rows as well

cards.subject: Normalisation
says: organises tables so each fact is stored once
reduces update, insert and delete anomalies
cards.use: see the same customer address copied into many rows
not: always makes reads faster

cards.subject: An update anomaly
says: leaves a fact inconsistent because one copy changed and the others did not
cards.use: change a customer's address in one order row but not in the rest
not: occurs only when a table has no primary key

cards.subject: An insertion anomaly
says: stops you recording one fact until an unrelated fact exists
appears when a new course cannot be stored until a student enrols
cards.use: cannot add a product to a table until someone has ordered it
not: is caused by a column holding too many NULLs

cards.subject: A deletion anomaly
says: loses an unrelated fact when the last row holding it is deleted
erases a supplier's details when its only order is removed
cards.use: lose a customer's address when their last order is deleted
not: is the same as a cascading delete working as designed

cards.subject: First normal form
says: requires each column to hold one atomic value
forbids repeating groups such as a comma-separated list in one column
cards.use: find a tags column holding 'red,blue,green'
not: requires every table to have a foreign key

cards.subject: Second normal form
says: requires every non-key column to depend on the whole of a composite key
is only in question when a table has a multi-column key
cards.use: see a column that depends on only one part of a two-column key
not: is about splitting values into atomic parts

cards.subject: Third normal form
says: forbids a non-key column from depending on another non-key column
moves a city-to-postcode style dependency into its own table
cards.use: see a column that is determined by another ordinary column rather than by the key
not: is satisfied by any table with a primary key

cards.subject: Denormalisation
says: deliberately duplicates data to avoid expensive joins
trades extra write work and drift risk for read speed
cards.use: have measured a slow join on a busy read path
not: is the same as a design with no keys

cards.subject: Boyce-Codd normal form
says: requires every determinant to be a candidate key
closes a gap third normal form can leave when candidate keys overlap
cards.use: meet a table with overlapping candidate keys that still shows an anomaly
not: is weaker than first normal form

cards.subject: A full table scan
says: reads every row to find matches
is perfectly acceptable on a tiny table
cards.use: see a query on a huge table read all of its rows
not: can only happen when an index is present

cards.subject: A B-tree index
says: keeps keys sorted in a balanced tree
supports equality, range and ORDER BY lookups
cards.use: need fast lookups and range filters on a column
not: answers only exact-match lookups

cards.subject: A unique index
says: enforces a rule while also speeding lookups on its columns
rejects a second row with the same key
cards.use: want to forbid duplicates and also look rows up quickly
not: slows reads but never helps them

cards.subject: A composite index
says: orders entries by its first column, then by the next
can serve queries that use its leftmost columns
cards.use: filter on two columns together in a hot query
not: serves a filter on its second column alone just as well

cards.subject: The leftmost prefix rule
says: explains why an index on (a, b) cannot reliably serve a filter on b alone
means column order in a composite index matters
cards.use: wonder why a user-only search ignores an index on (competition, user)
not: says the index must be created on the first column of the table

cards.subject: Index selectivity
says: is the share of distinct values in a column
makes a column worth indexing when it is high
cards.use: debate indexing a yes/no flag
not: is higher for a column with only two values

cards.subject: Over-indexing
says: slows every insert and update because each index must be maintained
wastes disk and memory on indexes no query uses
cards.use: see a write-heavy table with an index on every column
not: only affects SELECT statements

cards.subject: An index on a foreign key column
says: speeds joins from a parent to its children
speeds the check made when a parent row is deleted
cards.use: see a parent delete or join crawl because the child column has no index
not: is created automatically for you in SQLite

cards.subject: A covering index
says: contains every column the query needs so the table is never read
makes each index entry wider, so writes cost more
cards.use: want a hot query answered from the index alone
not: is another name for a unique index

cards.subject: A partial index
says: indexes only the rows that match a WHERE condition
stays small when few rows matter, such as unprocessed jobs
cards.use: need to look up only pending rows in a table that is mostly finished rows
not: indexes every row but compresses them

cards.subject: An index on an expression
says: indexes the result of a function such as lower(email)
is used only when the query writes the same expression
cards.use: need case-insensitive lookups on an indexed column
not: is used even when the query wraps the column in a different function

cards.subject: EXPLAIN
says: shows how the database intends to run a query
reveals whether an index will be used or the table scanned
cards.use: want to see why one query is slow
not: executes the query and returns its rows

cards.subject: The query planner
says: chooses the execution strategy for each query
estimates costs from table statistics
cards.use: wonder why the database picked one index over another
not: runs your statements in the order you wrote them

cards.subject: SELECT *
says: returns columns the caller never uses
defeats covering indexes
cards.use: see a query pull wide rows to display two fields
not: is always the fastest way to read a row

cards.subject: The N+1 query problem
says: runs one query for a list and then one more per row
is fixed with a join or a single batched query
cards.use: see a page issue hundreds of near-identical queries while rendering a list
not: happens only when a table has no index

cards.subject: OFFSET pagination
says: makes the database read and discard every skipped row
gets slower as the page number grows
cards.use: see page 5000 of a list take far longer than page 1
not: jumps straight to the requested page using the index

cards.subject: Keyset pagination
says: continues from the last key value the client saw
stays fast on deep pages
cards.use: need stable, fast paging through a large ordered list
not: lets users jump to an arbitrary page number cheaply

cards.subject: A sargable predicate
says: compares a bare indexed column to a value so the index can be used
is broken by wrapping the column in a function
cards.use: see an index ignored because the WHERE clause calls a function on the column
not: is any condition that uses an equals sign

cards.subject: A LIKE pattern with a leading wildcard
says: such as '%smith' prevents an ordinary index from narrowing the search
usually forces a scan of the whole table
cards.use: need to search for text that can appear anywhere in a column
not: is served efficiently by an ordinary index

cards.subject: A transaction
says: groups statements so they all succeed or all fail
ends with a commit or a rollback
cards.use: need a transfer to debit one account and credit another together
not: runs each statement in a separate commit

cards.subject: A rollback
says: discards every change made since the transaction began
cards.use: hit an error halfway through a multi-step change
not: makes the transaction's changes permanent

cards.subject: A commit
says: makes a transaction's changes permanent
makes them visible to other transactions
cards.use: finish all the steps of a change and want it kept
not: discards the changes made so far

cards.subject: Atomicity
says: means a transaction is applied entirely or not at all
cards.use: need a half-finished transfer never to be stored
not: means committed data survives a crash

cards.subject: Isolation
says: controls how far concurrent transactions can see each other's work
cards.use: worry that two users editing at once will see inconsistent data
not: means committed data survives a crash

cards.subject: Durability
says: means committed data survives a crash or power loss
cards.use: need a confirmed order to still exist after the server restarts
not: means a transaction is all-or-nothing

cards.subject: A dirty read
says: sees changes another transaction has not yet committed
can return data that is later rolled back
cards.use: read a balance that another session then rolls back
not: happens only under serializable isolation

cards.subject: A lost update
says: happens when two writers read the same value and the later write overwrites the earlier one
is avoided by atomic UPDATE expressions or version checks
cards.use: see two users editing the same record and one change silently vanish
not: is another name for a dirty read

cards.subject: A non-repeatable read
says: returns a different value when the same row is read twice in one transaction
happens when another transaction commits a change in between
cards.use: see a report disagree with itself within one transaction
not: means a row was read before it was committed

cards.subject: A phantom read
says: finds new rows matching a query appearing between two runs of it
concerns a set of rows rather than one row's value
cards.use: see a COUNT change between two runs inside one transaction
not: is caused by an uncommitted update

cards.subject: Serializable isolation
says: makes concurrent transactions behave as though they ran one at a time
is the strictest standard isolation level
cards.use: must stop write skew where two transactions each check a rule and both break it
not: allows dirty reads for speed

cards.subject: A deadlock
says: occurs when two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds
is resolved by aborting one of them as the victim
cards.use: see two jobs update the same two rows in opposite order and freeze
not: is cured by adding more indexes

cards.subject: Optimistic locking
says: checks a version number at update time and fails if the row changed
avoids holding locks while a user is thinking
cards.use: want to detect a lost update on a record edited through a web form
not: locks the row as soon as it is read

cards.subject: Pessimistic locking
says: locks the row up front so other writers must wait
suits short, high-contention updates
cards.use: expect many writers to fight over the same row
not: lets everyone read and write freely and only checks at the end

cards.subject: A migration
says: applies an ordered change to the database structure
is recorded so that it runs once
cards.use: need to change the schema in a reviewed and repeatable way
not: is a manual edit made directly on the production server

cards.subject: An additive change
says: adds a table or a nullable column without touching existing rows
is the safest kind of schema change on a live table
cards.use: want a low-risk change to a table that already holds data
not: removes data that is no longer needed

cards.subject: A destructive change
says: drops or reshapes existing columns or data
can lose rows that cannot be recovered without a backup
cards.use: are about to drop a column or change a type on a live table
not: only ever adds new columns

cards.subject: A NOT NULL column added with no default
says: cannot be added to a table that already has rows because they would have no value
is made safe by adding it as nullable, backfilling, then tightening
cards.use: need to add a required column to a table that already holds data
not: leaves existing rows with an empty string automatically

cards.subject: A backfill
says: fills a new column for rows that already exist
is best run in small batches so it does not hold long locks
cards.use: have just added a column and need old rows populated
not: is the step that removes the old column

cards.subject: Expand and contract
says: adds the new structure, migrates data, switches code, and removes the old structure in a later release
lets old and new application versions run against the same database
cards.use: need to rename a column on a live system without downtime
not: renames the column in one step during the deploy

cards.subject: A backward-compatible schema
says: works with both the old and the new version of the application
makes a rolling deploy safe
cards.use: run old and new app versions side by side during a deploy
not: requires stopping all traffic first

cards.subject: Schema drift
says: is the gap between the schema file and the live database
appears when someone changes production by hand
cards.use: find a column in production that no migration ever created
not: is the delay while a migration runs

cards.subject: A down migration
says: reverses a schema change
cannot bring back data that a dropped column already lost
cards.use: want a way to undo a release's schema change
not: is always lossless

cards.subject: The recovery point objective
says: states how much recent data you can afford to lose
sets how often backups must be taken
cards.use: must decide how often to back up
not: states how long you can afford to be down

cards.subject: The recovery time objective
says: states how long you can afford to be down
shapes how fast a restore must be
cards.use: must decide how quickly service has to return after a failure
not: states how much recent data you can afford to lose

cards.subject: A restore test
says: proves a backup can actually be recovered
turns a hope into evidence
cards.use: want to know whether last night's backup is any use
not: is unnecessary if the backup job reports success

cards.subject: An offsite copy
says: survives the loss of the machine or site holding the original
is stored on a different machine from the database
cards.use: worry that one disk failure would destroy both data and backups
not: is satisfied by a second folder on the same disk

cards.subject: A logical backup
says: exports data as SQL statements or rows
is portable across versions but slow to restore at scale
cards.use: need to move data between different engine versions
not: copies the raw database files

cards.subject: A physical backup
says: copies the database files or pages themselves
restores quickly but ties you to the engine and version
cards.use: need the fastest possible restore of a very large database
not: is a text file of INSERT statements

cards.subject: A consistent snapshot
says: captures data as of a single moment while writes continue
avoids half-applied changes in the copy
cards.use: need to back up a live database that is being written to
not: is made by copying files one at a time while the database runs

cards.subject: Point-in-time recovery
says: replays a log of changes onto a base backup to reach a chosen moment
can undo a bad delete that happened mid-morning
cards.use: need to restore to just before an accidental delete at 10:42
not: can only restore to the moment each nightly backup was taken

cards.subject: A replica
says: copies every change, including a mistaken delete, to the standby
improves availability but is not a backup
cards.use: think a standby server protects you from a dropped table
not: rolls back a bad change automatically

cards.subject: The 3-2-1 rule
says: keeps three copies on two kinds of media with one offsite
guards against a single failure destroying every copy
cards.use: want a simple checklist for how many copies to keep and where
not: says to keep one copy on three different disks in the same server

cards.subject: Backup encryption
says: protects copies at rest because they hold the same personal data as the live database
matters most for offsite copies
cards.use: store backups with a third party or on removable media
not: is unnecessary because backups are not personal data

cards.subject: A soft delete
says: marks a row deleted with a flag or timestamp instead of removing it
needs every query to filter out the marked rows
cards.use: want deleted records to be recoverable
not: removes the row permanently

cards.subject: A hard delete
says: removes the row permanently
frees the row's space for reuse
cards.use: must truly remove data once policy allows
not: leaves the row in place with a flag

cards.subject: A retention policy
says: states how long each kind of data is kept and why
gives deletion a rule instead of a guess
cards.use: ask how long old records should stay in the database
not: says to keep everything forever in case it is useful

cards.subject: Data archival
says: moves rarely used data out of hot tables while keeping it retrievable
keeps the working tables small and fast
cards.use: have years of old rows slowing the busiest tables
not: is the same as deleting the data

cards.subject: An audit trail
says: records who changed what and when
is append-only so history cannot be rewritten
cards.use: must show who altered a record last month
not: is a copy of the current rows only

cards.subject: Created and updated timestamps
says: record when a row was inserted and when it last changed
help debugging and incremental sync
cards.use: need to see when a row last changed
not: are filled in by the user on every form

cards.subject: A purge job
says: deletes expired rows on a schedule
works in small batches to avoid long locks
cards.use: must remove data that has passed its retention period
not: archives rows but never deletes them

cards.subject: A unique index limited to non-deleted rows
says: lets a soft-deleted row's value be reused
keeps active rows unique through a WHERE deleted_at IS NULL condition
cards.use: soft delete users but let a new user take the same email
not: blocks any reuse of a soft-deleted value

cards.subject: A legal hold
says: suspends deletion of named data while a dispute or investigation lasts
overrides the normal purge schedule
cards.use: are told that records tied to a dispute must not be purged
not: is a type of database lock

cards.subject: Personal data
says: is any information that identifies or can identify a person
includes email addresses and IP addresses
cards.use: need to decide whether a column falls under privacy rules
not: is limited to names and passwords

cards.subject: Data minimisation
says: collects only the fields the purpose requires
reduces what a breach can expose
cards.use: are tempted to store a birth date nobody needs
not: means collecting everything now in case it is useful later

cards.subject: Password hashing
says: stores a slow, salted one-way hash rather than the password
means a stolen table does not reveal the passwords directly
cards.use: must store credentials so they can be checked but not read
not: stores the password encrypted so it can be decrypted on demand

cards.subject: Encryption at rest
says: protects stored files and backups if a disk or copy is stolen
does not stop an authorised application user reading the data
cards.use: worry about a lost laptop or stolen backup drive
not: hides data from anyone who can log in to the app

cards.subject: A least-privilege database account
says: grants the application only the permissions it needs
limits the damage of a flaw such as SQL injection
cards.use: set up the account your app uses to connect
not: gives the app full administrator rights for convenience

cards.subject: Test data masking
says: replaces real personal values before production data reaches development
keeps realistic shapes without the real people
cards.use: want to copy production data into a test database
not: copies real customer data as it is

cards.subject: Pseudonymisation
says: replaces identifiers with tokens while the mapping is kept separately
still counts as personal data because it can be reversed
cards.use: need analysts to work on records without seeing names
not: makes the data permanently impossible to link to a person

cards.subject: Anonymisation
says: removes identifiability irreversibly so the data is no longer personal
cannot be undone by re-attaching a stored mapping
cards.use: want to keep statistics after a person's data must go
not: can be undone with a lookup table

cards.subject: An erasure request
says: requires locating a person's data across tables, exports and copies
is not satisfied by a soft-delete flag alone
cards.use: are asked by a user to delete their personal data
not: is met by hiding the account in the interface

cards.subject: A relational database
says: stores data in tables with defined columns and relationships
enforces constraints and supports joins
cards.use: need strong integrity rules across related records
not: stores each record as a free-form document with no schema

cards.subject: A document store
says: stores self-describing documents such as JSON
suits records whose shape varies from one item to the next
cards.use: hold items whose fields differ widely and are usually read whole
not: enforces foreign keys between collections

cards.subject: A key-value store
says: looks up a value by a single key
offers very fast simple reads but no joins
cards.use: need a cache or session lookup by a known key
not: supports joins across tables

cards.subject: A graph database
says: models data as nodes and edges
makes multi-hop traversals cheap
cards.use: need to find friends of friends several steps away
not: stores rows only in fixed columns

cards.subject: Polyglot persistence
says: uses different kinds of store for different jobs in one system
adds operational and consistency burden
cards.use: weigh adding a second database type for one feature
not: means running the same data in two identical databases

cards.subject: Shared-schema multi-tenancy
says: keeps every tenant's rows in the same tables with a tenant id column
relies on every query filtering by tenant
cards.use: serve many small customers cheaply from one database
not: gives each tenant a separate database file

cards.subject: Schema-per-tenant
says: gives each tenant its own set of tables inside one database
needs each migration applied to every schema
cards.use: need stronger separation than a tenant id column but one database server
not: puts all tenants into one set of tables

cards.subject: Database-per-tenant
says: gives each tenant a completely separate database
isolates tenants best but multiplies migrations and backups
cards.use: must keep one large customer's data physically separate
not: is the cheapest model when there are thousands of tenants

cards.subject: Row-level security
says: applies tenant filters inside the database so a missing WHERE cannot leak rows
moves isolation from application code into a policy
cards.use: fear a developer forgetting the tenant filter in a shared schema
not: is a feature present in every database engine

cards.subject: Sharding
says: splits one dataset across several databases by a shard key
makes cross-shard joins and transactions hard
cards.use: have outgrown what one machine can write
not: copies the full dataset to every node

cards.subject: A read replica
says: serves reads from a copy so the primary handles writes
may return slightly stale data
cards.use: need to take heavy reporting reads off the primary
not: accepts writes that sync back to the primary

cards.subject: A SQLite database
says: stores the whole database in a single file
runs inside the application process with no separate server
cards.use: want a database with no server to install
not: needs a daemon process listening on a port

cards.subject: The foreign_keys pragma
says: must be turned on for each connection before SQLite enforces foreign keys
is off by default
cards.use: find that child rows can point at missing parents
not: is stored permanently in the database file

cards.subject: Write-ahead logging
says: lets readers continue while one writer appends to a log file
is switched on with PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL
cards.use: see readers blocked while a writer works
not: allows many simultaneous writers

cards.subject: The SQLite write lock
says: allows only one writing transaction at a time
makes long write transactions block other writers
cards.use: see 'database is locked' under concurrent writes
not: is held per table so writers to different tables never wait

cards.subject: The busy_timeout pragma
says: makes a connection wait for a lock instead of failing at once
is set in milliseconds
cards.use: want a blocked writer to retry for a few seconds
not: increases the number of simultaneous writers

cards.subject: SQLite type affinity
says: lets a column accept a value of a different type than declared
means a declared INTEGER column is a preference, not a guarantee
cards.use: see text stored in an INTEGER column without an error
not: rejects any value of the wrong type

cards.subject: A STRICT table
says: enforces the declared column types
rejects a value that cannot be stored as the declared type
cards.use: want SQLite to reject text in an integer column
not: is the default for all tables

cards.subject: VACUUM INTO
says: writes a compacted, consistent copy of the database to a new file
can be run while the source database is in use
cards.use: need a consistent copy of a live SQLite file
not: deletes the source database after copying

cards.subject: The enroll_unique index
says: stops a learner enrolling in the same track twice
covers user and track
holds even when two requests race
cards.use: need to explain why duplicate enrolments are impossible in GGLearn
not: is enforced only by the enrolment page's code

cards.subject: The questions_dedupe index
says: makes a question unique per track, level and prompt
keeps a repeated import from creating copies
cards.use: import the same question bank twice and expect no duplicates
not: deletes the older questions first

cards.subject: The certificate unique index
says: allows one certificate per user, track and level
cards.use: need to know how GGLearn avoids issuing the same certificate twice
not: allows one certificate per user across all tracks

cards.subject: The competition members unique index
says: stops a user joining the same competition twice
leads with the competition column
cards.use: need to know how a user is kept from joining a competition twice
not: leads with the user column

cards.subject: The cm_user_lookup index
says: speeds the page that lists which competitions a user is in
exists because the unique index on competition and user cannot serve a user-only search
cards.use: wonder why a second index exists on the competition members table
not: duplicates the unique index to enforce the same rule

cards.subject: GGLearn's foreign_keys setting
says: is switched on when the database connection opens
is needed because SQLite does not enforce foreign keys unless asked
cards.use: wonder why GGLearn's connection code sets a pragma
not: is turned on by running drizzle-kit push

cards.subject: The GGLearn schema file
says: is lib/db/schema.ts
defines the tables with Drizzle for SQLite
is what drizzle-kit push compares with the live database
cards.use: need to find where GGLearn's tables are defined
not: is a set of numbered SQL migration files

cards.subject: A user's role in GGLearn
says: is stored once on the user row and read each time
avoids stale copies of the role in sessions
cards.use: wonder where GGLearn keeps a person's role
not: is copied into every session at sign-in and trusted afterwards

cards.subject: GGLearn's SQLite file during deploy
says: is excluded from the rsync so a release never overwrites live data
is never replaced by the copy in the repository
cards.use: wonder how GGLearn deploys avoid wiping learner data
not: is overwritten by the repository copy on each deploy

cards.subject: The drizzle-kit push step in the GGLearn deploy
says: runs without --force
stops and fails the deploy if a change would delete rows
cards.use: wonder how GGLearn guards against a schema change destroying data
not: runs with --force so the schema always matches

cards.subject: Push ordering in ggsocial
says: runs the schema push before the app restarts
prevents the new build querying columns that do not exist yet
cards.use: wonder why ggsocial applies the schema before restarting
not: restarts the app first so users see no downtime
like: The drizzle-kit push step in the GGLearn deploy

cards.subject: ggmoney migration files
says: are kept as numbered files in db/migrations
are run by bin/migrate.php rather than by a schema-diff tool
cards.use: need to know how ggmoney changes its schema
not: are generated by drizzle-kit push

cards.subject: The bin/migrate.php script
says: applies only the migrations still pending
is safe to run repeatedly
cards.use: need to know whether running ggmoney's migrate script twice is harmful
not: drops and recreates all tables on each run

cards.subject: The bin/backup.php script
says: runs nightly from cron
uses mysqldump for MySQL and VACUUM INTO for SQLite
cards.use: need to know how ggmoney's backup is scheduled
not: runs only when an operator starts it by hand

cards.subject: The ggmoney six-year rule
says: applies to statutory accounting records
is the reason ggmoney backs up nightly
cards.use: wonder why ggmoney treats its data as long-lived
not: allows accounting records to be purged after one year

cards.subject: The mysqldump --single-transaction option
says: takes a consistent snapshot without blocking writes
is what ggmoney's backup uses for MySQL
cards.use: need to back up ggmoney's MySQL data while the app is running
not: locks every table for the length of the dump

cards.subject: ggmoney local snapshots
says: number thirty daily copies
are stated plainly not to be an offsite backup
cards.use: wonder how safe ggmoney's backups are against losing the server
not: are copied offsite automatically

cards.subject: The ggsocial pre-deploy backup
says: copies the database to /root/ggsocial-backups
runs before anything is changed
cards.use: need to know where ggsocial's database is saved before a deploy
not: runs after the schema push to confirm it worked

qa.q: What does PRIMARY KEY on id guarantee in this table?
qa.right: No two rows can share the same id
wrong: Every other column also becomes unique
The id column is encrypted on disk
No other table may refer to this table
qa.why: A primary key identifies each row uniquely and is what other tables point at.

qa.q: A rating column must only ever hold 1 to 5. Which definition makes the database enforce that?
qa.right: rating INTEGER CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5)
wrong: rating INTEGER DEFAULT 5
rating INTEGER NOT NULL
rating INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
qa.why: A CHECK constraint rejects rows whose values fail the stated condition.

qa.q: After this runs, what is account 1's balance compared with before?
qa.right: Unchanged, because the change was rolled back
wrong: Reduced by 100
Reduced by 100 and logged
The statement fails and locks the table
qa.why: ROLLBACK discards everything done since BEGIN.

qa.q: Is this schema change safe on a live table that already has rows?
qa.right: Yes, it is additive and existing rows are untouched
wrong: No, it rewrites every row and locks the table for hours
No, it deletes the oldest rows
Yes, but only after dropping the table
qa.code: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN nickname TEXT;
qa.why: Adding a nullable column does not change existing rows.

qa.q: What happens on the second INSERT?
qa.right: It fails with a unique constraint error
wrong: It silently updates the first row
It succeeds and creates a duplicate
It deletes the first row and inserts a new one
qa.why: A unique index makes a duplicate impossible, even with racing requests.

qa.q: Which query lists only the users who are not soft-deleted?
qa.right: SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
wrong: SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at = NULL;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at = 0;
SELECT * FROM users HAVING deleted_at;
qa.why: NULL is tested with IS NULL; comparing with = NULL is never true.

qa.q: Why does this query return no rows even though some users are active?
qa.right: Comparing to NULL with = is never true, so the condition matches nothing
wrong: The table has no index on deleted_at
WHERE cannot be used with timestamps
The query needs a GROUP BY
qa.code: SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at = NULL;
qa.why: Use IS NULL; = NULL evaluates to unknown.

qa.q: What does the first line of this plan tell you?
qa.right: The query reads every row of orders
wrong: The query uses a covering index
The query is cached
The table has no primary key
qa.why: SCAN means a full table scan; SEARCH ... USING INDEX means an index was used.

qa.q: Which statement best speeds up frequent lookups by email?
qa.right: CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);
wrong: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN email_fast TEXT;
CREATE VIEW users_by_email AS SELECT * FROM users;
VACUUM;
qa.why: An index on the filtered column lets the database search instead of scan.

qa.q: With foreign_keys ON, what happens to order_lines rows for order 1 after this delete?
qa.right: They are deleted too
wrong: They stay and point at nothing
The delete fails
They are moved to order 0
qa.why: ON DELETE CASCADE removes child rows with the parent.

qa.q: A fresh SQLite connection runs this insert and there is no order 99. What happens?
qa.right: It succeeds, because foreign key checks are off by default
wrong: It fails with a foreign key error
SQLite creates order 99
It is queued until order 99 exists
qa.code: INSERT INTO order_lines (order_id) VALUES (99);
qa.why: SQLite enforces foreign keys only after PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON.

qa.q: A post has many comments. Where does the foreign key go?
qa.right: On the comments table, as post_id
wrong: On the posts table, as comment_id
In a third junction table only
In both tables
qa.why: In a one-to-many relationship the foreign key sits on the many side.

qa.q: Students take many courses and courses have many students. What is the standard design?
qa.right: A junction table with a foreign key to each side
wrong: A comma-separated course list in the students table
One column per course on the students table
A foreign key from courses to the first student
qa.why: A many-to-many relationship needs a link table.

qa.q: A team's nightly backup job reports success every day and nobody has restored from it. What is the best next step?
qa.right: Restore a recent backup into a test copy and check the data
wrong: Do nothing, since the job reports success
Make the job run twice a night
Compress the backups more
qa.why: Only a restore proves a backup works.

qa.q: Backups run at 02:00 and the server fails at 17:00. What is the most recent data you can recover?
qa.right: Everything up to 02:00, so up to 15 hours of changes are lost
wrong: Everything up to 16:59
Everything up to the previous midnight
Nothing, because backups cannot restore data
qa.why: The recovery point is the time of the last good backup.

qa.q: Which filter can this composite index narrow directly from its leftmost column?
qa.right: WHERE user_id = 3
wrong: WHERE track_id = 7
WHERE track_id IN (1, 2)
WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'
qa.code: CREATE INDEX ix_enroll ON enrollments (user_id, track_id);
qa.why: A composite index serves queries that start from its first column.

qa.q: A team has an index on users(email) but this query still scans. Why?
qa.right: The function on the column stops the plain index being used; index lower(email) or store it normalised
wrong: Indexes cannot be used with WHERE
lower() is not allowed in SQLite
The index must be rebuilt after every query
qa.code: SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'a@x.com';
qa.why: Wrapping an indexed column in a function makes the predicate non-sargable.

qa.q: A page renders 200 posts and the log shows 201 queries. What is the problem and the fix?
qa.right: N+1 queries; fetch the authors with one join or one batched query
wrong: A missing primary key; add one
Too few indexes; index every column
The database is too small; add a replica
qa.why: One query for the list plus one per row is the N+1 pattern.

qa.q: Why does this query get slower on later pages?
qa.right: The database has to read and discard all the skipped rows first
wrong: LIMIT disables the index
OFFSET sorts rows in reverse
The result is cached per page
qa.code: SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;
qa.why: OFFSET cost grows with the number of rows skipped; keyset pagination avoids it.

qa.q: A script inserts 50,000 rows into SQLite with a separate commit for each and takes minutes. What is the best fix?
qa.right: Wrap the inserts in a single BEGIN ... COMMIT
wrong: Add an index on every column
Run the inserts from several processes at once
Switch the column types to TEXT
qa.why: Each commit forces a sync to disk; one transaction pays that cost once.

qa.q: Transaction A updates a row and later rolls back. Transaction B read the new value before the rollback. What was B's problem?
qa.right: A dirty read
wrong: A phantom read
A deadlock
A lost update
qa.why: Reading uncommitted data that is later discarded is a dirty read.

qa.q: Why is the first form safer than the second when two requests run at once?
qa.right: The database applies the subtraction to the current value atomically; the second can overwrite another request's change
wrong: The first uses fewer bytes on the wire
The second is not valid SQL
The first skips constraint checks
qa.why: A read-modify-write in the app can produce a lost update.

qa.q: A migration adds a required column with no default to a table that already has rows. In SQLite, what happens?
qa.right: It is refused; add a default or add the column as nullable and backfill
wrong: Existing rows get an empty string
The existing rows are deleted
It works but locks the table forever
qa.code: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN plan TEXT NOT NULL;
qa.why: Existing rows would have no value for a NOT NULL column.

qa.q: A team must populate a new column for 20 million existing rows on a live system. What should they do?
qa.right: Backfill in small batches
wrong: Run one UPDATE for all rows in the busiest hour
Drop the table and reload it
Skip the backfill and leave the column empty forever
qa.why: Small batches avoid long locks and let the system keep serving users.

qa.q: Users are soft-deleted with deleted_at. What does this index allow?
qa.right: A new user can reuse the email of a soft-deleted user while active emails stay unique
wrong: Two active users can share an email
Soft-deleted users are removed from disk
Emails become case-insensitive
qa.code:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_active
  ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
qa.why: A partial unique index applies only where deleted_at IS NULL.

qa.q: A support person says 'what changed on this record last week and who did it?'. Which design answers it?
qa.right: An append-only audit table with actor, time, and before and after values
wrong: A single updated_at column
The current row with no history
A comment field edited by whoever last changed the record
qa.why: An audit trail records who, when and what, and should not be rewritable.

qa.q: A SaaS app uses one shared schema with a tenant_id column. What is wrong with this query?
qa.right: It never filters by tenant, so a guessed id could return another tenant's invoice
wrong: It uses SELECT *
It should use OFFSET
The id column must be text
qa.code: SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ?;
qa.why: Every query in a shared schema must be scoped by tenant_id.

qa.q: Deleting a parent row is slow and the child table's foreign key column has no index. What is the likely cause?
qa.right: The database scans the child table to find referencing rows
wrong: The parent has too many columns
Foreign keys always lock the database
The child table has too few rows
qa.why: An index on the foreign key column speeds the delete check and joins.

qa.q: A developer wants production data to test with. What is the safest approach?
qa.right: Copy it only after masking personal values
wrong: Copy it as it is to a laptop
Share the production password with the team
Disable the production constraints and test there
qa.why: Masking keeps realistic shapes without exposing real people.

qa.q: How should an app store user passwords?
qa.right: As a slow, salted one-way hash
wrong: Encrypted so support can read them back
As plain text in a restricted table
As a fast unsalted checksum
qa.why: Hashing allows checking a password without being able to read it.

qa.q: The query below is answered from the index alone. What makes that possible?
qa.right: The index contains customer_id and total, so it covers the query
wrong: total is the primary key
The table has no rows
SQLite caches the result
qa.code:
CREATE INDEX ix_orders ON orders (customer_id, total);
SELECT total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 5;
qa.why: A covering index holds every column the query needs.

qa.q: A report reads the same row twice in one transaction and gets different values. Which setting prevents that?
qa.right: Repeatable read or stricter isolation
wrong: Read uncommitted
Dropping the transaction
Turning off constraints
qa.why: A non-repeatable read is prevented by repeatable read and serializable isolation.

qa.q: A live app with two servers deployed one after the other must rename users.fullname to users.display_name. What should the team do?
qa.right: Add display_name, write both, backfill, switch reads, and drop fullname in a later release
wrong: Rename the column in the same deploy as the code change
Stop all traffic and rename by hand in production
Create a new database and abandon the old one
qa.why: Expand and contract keeps old and new versions working during the deploy.

qa.q: A SQLite app has slow reads while a nightly job writes. Which change usually helps?
qa.right: Switch to write-ahead logging
wrong: Turn off foreign keys
Add a second writer process
Move the file to a USB drive
qa.code: PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
qa.why: WAL lets readers continue while a writer appends to the log.

qa.q: A SQLite app throws 'database is locked' whenever two requests write at once. What is the most sensible first fix?
qa.right: Set a busy timeout and keep write transactions short
wrong: Open a new database file per request
Disable the journal
Remove every index
qa.code: PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;
qa.why: SQLite allows one writer; waiting briefly and holding the lock briefly avoids most failures.

qa.q: A bad DELETE ran at 10:42 and the last nightly backup is from 02:00. Change logs have been archived. What recovers the most data?
qa.right: Restore the 02:00 backup and replay the log to just before 10:42
wrong: Restore the 02:00 backup and accept the loss
Restore the replica
Run the delete again with a WHERE clause
qa.why: Point-in-time recovery replays changes onto a base backup up to a chosen moment.

qa.q: Someone drops a table on the primary and the replica drops it too. What should the team do?
qa.right: Restore from a backup, because a replica copies mistakes
wrong: Fail over to the replica, which still has the table
Wait for the replica to resync
Recreate the table empty and carry on
qa.why: A replica copies every change, including mistakes; it is not a backup.

qa.q: Deleting a customer cascades to their orders, but finance must keep invoices. What is the best fix?
qa.right: Use RESTRICT and soft-delete or anonymise the customer instead
wrong: Keep CASCADE and export the orders first
Remove the foreign key
Delete the finance rules
qa.why: Cascade can erase records you are required to keep.

qa.q: Which query pages forward fast through a large table?
qa.right: SELECT * FROM events WHERE id < ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;
wrong: SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET ?;
SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY RANDOM() LIMIT 20;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events;
qa.why: Keyset pagination continues from the last seen key and avoids skipping rows.

qa.q: A user asks for deletion of their account. The app only sets deleted_at. What is the problem?
qa.right: Their personal data still exists in the table
wrong: The row is too large
Soft delete is illegal
The user cannot sign up again
qa.why: A flag hides the row but does not remove the personal data.

qa.q: After loading millions of rows the database starts choosing poor query plans. What is a likely cause and fix?
qa.right: Stale statistics; refresh them with ANALYZE
wrong: Too many columns; drop the table
The index is full; delete it
The database is encrypted
qa.why: The planner relies on statistics, which go stale after bulk loads.

qa.q: A comment count column often disagrees with the real number of comments. What is the best fix?
qa.right: Update the counter in the same transaction as the change
wrong: Run a nightly job and accept the drift
Remove the foreign key
Cache the page for a day
qa.why: A derived value should change in the same transaction as its source.

qa.q: Two jobs each lock rows A and B in opposite order and freeze. What fix is standard?
qa.right: Take locks in a consistent order and retry the aborted transaction
wrong: Add an index to both tables
Run both jobs at once on purpose
Raise the isolation level to read uncommitted
qa.why: A consistent lock order prevents the circular wait.

qa.q: This update affects 0 rows. What does that tell you?
qa.right: Another writer changed the row since you read it, so reload or report a conflict
wrong: The query has a syntax error
The row was inserted twice
The database is read-only
qa.why: With optimistic locking a version mismatch means someone else updated first.

qa.q: Why is this index small and fast for a job queue where most rows are done?
qa.right: It indexes only the pending rows
wrong: It indexes only the oldest rows
It compresses the whole table
It makes status unique
qa.code: CREATE INDEX jobs_pending ON jobs (run_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
qa.why: A partial index covers only rows matching its WHERE condition.

qa.q: Developers keep forgetting the tenant filter in a shared schema. What is the strongest systemic fix?
qa.right: Enforce isolation in the database (row-level security or a mandatory scoped query layer) and test it
wrong: Ask developers to be more careful
Rely on code review alone
Switch every column to TEXT
qa.why: Moving isolation out of each individual query removes the human failure mode.

qa.q: Comments attach to posts or photos through commentable_type and commentable_id. What is the integrity weakness?
qa.right: The database cannot enforce a foreign key on the polymorphic pair
wrong: Comments cannot be sorted
It forces a junction table
Text columns cannot be indexed
qa.why: A type-plus-id pair cannot be a real foreign key; separate nullable keys with a CHECK or separate link tables can be.

qa.q: In SQLite, what does this return?
qa.right: text
wrong: integer
null
an error is raised
qa.why: Without STRICT, type affinity stores a non-convertible value as text.

qa.q: Two on-call doctors each check that at least one other doctor is on call, then both go off call. What anomaly is this and what prevents it?
qa.right: Write skew; serializable isolation or locking the shared rule
wrong: A dirty read; read uncommitted
A phantom delete; a bigger disk
A lost index; a covering index
qa.why: Each transaction read a state the other then invalidated.

qa.q: A nightly backup job exits with code 0 but the files are only a few bytes. What gap does this expose?
qa.right: No check of backup size, integrity or restorability
wrong: The server clock is wrong
The files should be compressed more
Backups should run during the day
qa.why: Monitor backup output and restore regularly.

qa.q: A team's backup script copies the live SQLite file with cp while the app is writing. What is the risk and the better approach?
qa.right: The copy can be inconsistent; use VACUUM INTO or the online backup API
wrong: No risk; cp is atomic
It deletes the live file; use mv
It only misses the indexes
qa.why: A plain copy of a database in use may capture a half-written state.

qa.q: In GGLearn, learners reported duplicate enrolments after a double-click. Why can the database still guarantee uniqueness?
qa.right: A unique index on user and track rejects the second insert even if two requests race
wrong: The button is disabled in the page
Sessions are single-threaded
Enrolments are deleted nightly
qa.why: A database constraint cannot be bypassed by racing requests.

qa.q: A GGLearn deploy fails because the schema change would delete rows. What is the right response?
qa.right: Do not force it; back up, use steps to move the data, and remove the old column in a later release
wrong: Rerun with --force immediately
Skip the schema push forever
Delete the failing table and let push recreate it
qa.why: The deploy refuses destructive pushes on purpose.

qa.q: ggsocial's new build queries a column that the schema push has not created yet. What ordering mistake caused it?
qa.right: The app was restarted before the schema push ran
wrong: The push ran before the restart
The database was backed up first
The column was nullable
qa.why: Schema should be applied before the new build serves traffic.

qa.q: A new GGLearn page must list the competitions a user is in, and the competition members table is only indexed on (competition, user). What should be added?
qa.right: A separate index on user
wrong: A second copy of the table
A unique index on competition alone
Nothing, the composite index covers it
qa.why: A composite index does not serve searches that skip its first column; GGLearn added cm_user_lookup.

qa.q: Why does the GGLearn rsync deploy exclude the SQLite file?
qa.right: So a release never overwrites live learner data
wrong: Because SQLite files are too large
Because rsync cannot copy binary files
To speed up compilation
qa.why: The live database must survive deploys untouched.

qa.q: ggmoney's nightly job backs up SQLite with VACUUM INTO instead of copying the file. Why?
qa.right: It gives a consistent snapshot of a database in use
wrong: It encrypts the file
It makes backups offsite
It is the only way to compress files
qa.why: A plain copy may be inconsistent while writes continue.

qa.q: A reviewer notes ggmoney keeps 30 daily snapshots on the same server. What weakness should be fixed first?
qa.right: Add an offsite copy, since a lost server takes the snapshots with it
wrong: Keep fewer snapshots
Back up more often locally
Encrypt the cron job
qa.why: Local copies do not survive loss of the machine.

qa.q: ggmoney must keep accounting records for six years, and a developer proposes a purge job that deletes anything older than two years. What should happen?
qa.right: Reject it; the retention rule must come before the purge
wrong: Approve it to save space
Run it only on weekends
Move the purge into the application
qa.why: Delete only when policy allows.

qa.q: A migration needs to change a column type on a live table of 100 million rows. Which approach is safest?
qa.right: Add a new column, backfill in batches, switch code to it, then drop the old column later
wrong: ALTER the type in place during peak hours
Drop the table and rebuild from backup
Change the type in the application only
qa.why: Expand and contract avoids a long lock and keeps rollback possible.
